headline: High-risk filesystem and action overlap: Open Interpreter and OpenHands both default to broad shell, write, and network access, creating dangerous conflict and cascading-error pathways.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Both agents can read and write files, and Open Interpreter explicitly shares state via filesystem while OpenHands operates on mounted runtime files. That creates a plausible content-to-instruction bridge if one agent processes the other's files or outputs as trusted text. No MCP/shared-message channel is documented, so this is not high.
conditions: IF either agent reads the other agent's generated files as instructions without provenance checks
IF a shared directory is used for handoff between the two agents
mitigations: Separate their working directories immediately
Disable automatic execution of file contents in both agents
Add a manual review step before either agent consumes the other's outputs
Use read-only mounts for handoff artifacts
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging for inter-agent files

B_data_leakage.rationale: Open Interpreter can access the entire user filesystem and has broad network egress; OpenHands can read files in its runtime sandbox and also use model-provider APIs and MCP servers. If sensitive files are mounted or copied into OpenHands, either agent can expose them through outbound model/API calls. The pair therefore has a default leakage path, though not enough evidence for critical.
conditions: IF sensitive files are placed in OpenHands' mounted runtime
IF Open Interpreter is pointed at directories containing secrets or regulated data
IF either agent forwards file contents to a third-party model provider
mitigations: Keep secrets out of both working directories
Rotate or redact credentials before handing files to either agent
Restrict OpenHands mounts to minimal project subtrees
Run both agents with separate API keys
requires-engineering: enforce DLP or content filtering on outbound prompts

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents have unrestricted filesystem write, shell execution, package installation, and git-state modification. Open Interpreter shares state via filesystem, while OpenHands shares state via mounted volume, so concurrent edits to the same repo or directory can race and corrupt files or git history. This matches the high-severity overlap indicator because both can mutate the same mutable resources without documented locking.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same repository or directory
IF both agents modify git state without an external lock
IF mounted volumes expose the same writable path to both runtimes
mitigations: Assign each agent a separate checkout
Serialize writes with a manual lock file
Pause one agent before the other edits shared files
Use branch-per-agent workflows
requires-engineering: add filesystem locking or transactional merge orchestration

D_cascading_error.rationale: Open Interpreter can generate shell commands, edits, and file-based outputs that OpenHands may then act on inside its agent loop. Because OpenHands has browser, shell, and MCP-enabled action capability, unverified outputs from Open Interpreter can cascade into real actions. The pair lacks a documented verification barrier, so the default pathway is dangerous.
conditions: IF OpenHands consumes Open Interpreter output as authoritative task input
IF Open Interpreter emits commands or facts that are not independently verified
IF OpenHands is allowed to execute browser or shell actions from that input
mitigations: Require human approval before OpenHands acts on Open Interpreter output
Insert a verification step that checks commands against source files
Limit Open Interpreter to drafting only, not execution
Log and diff all proposed actions before execution
requires-engineering: build a typed handoff schema with validation

E_compliance.rationale: Open Interpreter can touch anything reachable on the local machine, while OpenHands processes files mounted into its runtime and may send prompts to configured model providers. If regulated data is present in the local filesystem or mounted workspace, the pair can create retention and residency mismatches through duplicated copies and outbound API processing. The profiles do not specify HIPAA/GDPR certifications, so uncertainty keeps this at medium rather than high.
conditions: IF regulated data is stored in the local filesystem or mounted runtime
IF either agent's provider retains prompts or file contents longer than policy allows
IF the same data class is processed by both agents under different retention rules
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of both agents' working sets
Use separate retention policies for each runtime
Review provider logging settings before use
Purge temporary files after each session
requires-engineering: document residency and retention controls per agent
